title: Life of a Request & REST Design
caps: get slash users slash forty two
slash orders slash nine ninety nine

scenes.say: You click, and a database row shows up in about a quarter of a second. Where did it go? You'll trace every hop, and design an API that survives a retry with no double charge.
Today you will do three things. Trace a request from click to database. Design REST routes with honest status codes. And make retries safe with an idempotency key.
lines: Trace a request from click to database
Design REST routes with honest codes

scenes.title: What happens when you call an API?
scenes.statement: A browser calls an endpoint and gets JSON back, a text format for data. Name every hop (each stop the request makes) and where the time goes.
scenes.say: A browser calls an endpoint and gets JSON back, a text format for data. For example, get users forty two. We want every hop, each stop it makes, and the time each takes.

scenes.head: A restaurant in disguise
scenes.say: Picture a restaurant. The diner is the client. The host desk sends the order to a free kitchen: the load balancer. The kitchen cooks: your app server. For ingredients, it goes to the pantry: the database.

scenes.head: GET /users/42, hop by hop
scenes.say: The browser wants get slash users slash forty two. It asks DNS for the server's address, like a phone book. Then it opens a TCP connection, a reliable pipe between two machines, and a TLS handshake encrypts it. The load balancer picks one healthy server. The app runs your handler, the function for this path. It sends one SQL query, a question to the database. The row comes back, and the app answers two hundred with JSON. Same journey as the restaurant: diner, host desk, kitchen, pantry.

scenes.head: Time each hop with curl
scenes.say: Time each stage with curl. Put three timers in a format file, then run curl with it. Each number is cumulative, in seconds. DNS was done at twenty milliseconds. TLS was done at one fifty five. The first byte arrived at two forty. The gap between two numbers is what that stage cost.
Your turn. Using those numbers, how long did you spend waiting for the server, between TLS finishing and the first byte arriving? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: TLS done at 0.155 s, first byte at 0.240 s. Time spent waiting for the server?

scenes.head: Where 240 ms went
scenes.say: Eighty five: two forty minus one fifty five. By stage, DNS cost twenty. Connecting and encrypting cost a hundred thirty five, the biggest slice. The wait for the first byte, server time plus one round trip, was eighty five.

scenes.head: Inside the app: 404 or 200
scenes.say: Inside the app, the router matches the path and calls your function, the handler. One query goes to the database. No row? Four oh four. Otherwise it turns the row into JSON and answers two hundred. Forty two exists. Seven doesn't.

setup.app.py:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("create table users(id integer, name text)")
db.execute("insert into users values (42, 'Ada')")

scenes.head: Follow-ups on the journey
scenes.say: That answers our problem. Follow ups. Why a load balancer? To spread traffic and survive a dead server. Why TLS? It encrypts, and proves who the server is. It's slow? Time each hop, then fix the biggest. The mistake: skipping DNS and TLS, and saying only that the server returns JSON.

scenes.title: Design the API for orders
scenes.statement: Design the URLs, methods and status codes of an orders service so any client can guess them.

example.input: create, read, replace, delete an order
example.output: nouns in paths, honest status codes

scenes.say: Say we build the orders service. The problem: design the URLs, methods and codes. For example, create, read, replace, delete. We want nouns in paths and honest codes.

scenes.head: A filing cabinet
scenes.say: Picture a filing cabinet. One drawer holds all orders, slash orders. One folder inside is order forty two. The path names the drawer or the folder. The verb says what you do: read it, add one, or replace it. Nouns in the path, verbs in the method. That's REST.

notes.text: nouns in paths, verbs in methods

scenes.head: Methods and success codes
scenes.say: Use plural nouns: orders, not get orders. Get reads and never changes anything. Post creates a new order, and answers two oh one Created. Put replaces the whole order. Patch changes only a few fields. Delete removes it, with two oh four and no body. A duplicate post gets four oh nine, Conflict.
Your turn. A client posts an order that already exists. Which status should come back? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `POST /orders` with an item that already exists. Status?

scenes.head: Status codes as code
scenes.say: Four oh nine, Conflict. Watch the code decide. No item in the body? Four hundred: the caller got it wrong. The item already exists? Four oh nine. Otherwise two oh one, Created. Three calls print four hundred, four oh nine, two oh one.

scenes.head: Codes on the request path
scenes.say: Here are the codes on one picture. Two oh one: the post worked. Four hundred: bad input. Four oh four: missing, the path is fine but the thing isn't there. Four oh nine: it already exists, a clash. All four hundreds mean the caller was wrong.

scenes.head: Follow-ups on REST design
scenes.say: That is the orders API: nouns in paths, honest codes. Follow ups. Four oh one or four oh three? Not logged in, versus not allowed. Five hundreds? The server broke, our fault. Put or patch? Put replaces everything, patch only the fields sent. Versioning? A v one prefix, and never break old clients. Mistake: verbs in paths, two hundred for everything.
rows: Not logged in vs. not allowed
PUT replaces all; PATCH only fields sent

scenes.title: A retry that double-charges
scenes.statement: A client times out and retries a POST that actually worked. Don't create two orders.
scenes.say: Now the nasty one. A client times out, and retries a post that actually worked. For example, post orders twice for one purchase. We want exactly one order.

scenes.head: One purchase, two orders
scenes.say: A shopper taps pay. The client calls the server with post slash orders. The server saves the order. But the answer is lost on a bad connection, and the client sees a timeout. So it retries, sending the same post again. The server saves a second order. Two orders, one purchase, one angry customer.

scenes.head: The naive server
scenes.say: The same thing in code. Post appends an order and returns two oh one. The retry calls it again. Print the count: two orders, exactly like the picture.

panels.code:
orders = []
def post_order(item):
    orders.append(item)
    return 201
post_order("book")
post_order("book")
print(len(orders))

scenes.say: Now a different method. A client retries put slash orders slash forty two, with the same body, three times. How many orders exist afterwards? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `PUT /orders/42`, same body, sent 3 times. Orders stored?

scenes.head: Is a retry safe?
scenes.say: One. Put sets a state, so doing it three times leaves the same end state. That's idempotent. Get and delete are idempotent too. Post isn't, so a retry makes two orders. The fix is an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key, and the server replays the first result for repeats.

scenes.head: Replay the first result
scenes.say: Now the server remembers keys. The first call with key k one is new, so it saves the order and records two oh one. The retry has the same key, so the server replays that answer and saves nothing. One order. The client makes a fresh key for each purchase. That solves the double charge: same key, same answer, one order.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What happens on a call? DNS finds the address, then TCP and TLS connect. Then the balancer picks a server, and the app queries the database. Back comes two hundred with JSON. Where does the time go? DNS, connecting, and waiting. I time each with curl. Slow? I fix the biggest slice.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How do you design a REST API? Plural nouns in paths, verbs as methods: get reads, post creates. Then honest codes. Two oh one, created. Four hundred, bad input. Four oh four, missing. Four oh nine, a clash.

items.text: Plural nouns in paths, verbs as methods

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Two more four hundreds. Four oh one, not logged in: who are you? Four oh three, logged in but not allowed. And five hundreds? The server broke. That's our fault, not the caller's.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is idempotent? Doing it twice leaves the same end state as once. Get, put and delete are. Post isn't. A retried post? Send an idempotency key, and the server replays the first result. Put or patch? Put replaces all, patch only the fields sent. Versioning? A v one prefix.

scenes.head: Practice this week
scenes.say: Three exercises. Run curl with the timing format on a real site, and name the biggest slice. Sketch five routes for a library API, with the status code for each. And write a post that takes an idempotency key, then replay it.

scenes.say: So say this. DNS, TCP, TLS, balancer, app, database. I time each hop. Nouns in paths, verbs as methods, honest status codes. Post isn't idempotent, so retries carry an idempotency key.
